data.title: More than 100 Democratic operatives urge party leaders to reject AI cash
data.description:
More than 170 Democratic organizers and campaign staff members are calling on the party’s leaders to reject campaign donations from the pro-artificial intelligence super PAC Leading the Future (LTF) as the debate over AI safety and regulations intensifies in Washington.

The letter, first shared with The Hill on Friday, argues the millions of dollars from AI industry executives is “fundamentally at odds with the Democratic Party’s core values.”

“We are a party that values people over unchecked regressive power, that believes in the role of government in reining in corporate greed and that advocates for accountability and fairness in our economy,” the letter states.

Leading the Future is at the center of the AI industry’s campaign spending push. It has received millions from OpenAI President Greg Brockman, the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, AI firm Perplexity and venture capitalist Joe Lonsdale. 

Ezra Andres-Tysch, a Democratic strategist who helped organize the letter, said he hopes the letter “makes it easier for someone to go to their their campaign manager or their candidate and say, why are we doing this?”

“Why are we, you know, taking money from these campaigns? Why are we holding these positions that aren’t popular?” he added.

“One of the reasons that I hope that this kind of breaks through is often campaign staff are that connection line to a candidate,” Andres-Tysch told The Hill. “I think often candidates live in their own little worlds, and then the campaign staff who are knocking on doors, talking to real people, can be that canary in a coal mine.”

It comes as concerns mount over the future of AI development and its potential impacts on jobs, the environment and national security. Earlier this week, more than a dozen Democratic congressional candidates started a new push to call on campaigns to refuse LTF’s money.

LTF has raised at least $140 million for the 2026 midterm election cycle. The spending group has donated to members on both sides of the aisle, maintaining its goal to “support a well-balanced, cross-partisan conversation about artificial intelligence.”

This “starts with passing a strong and thoughtful national regulatory framework,” the super PAC said in a statement earlier this year. “Our north star is to support a political environment where policymakers at the federal and state levels can tune out the extremes and engage thoughtfully on critical policy issues surrounding innovation in and adoption of AI.”

The super PAC says a framework should include safety protections for kids, baseline safety standards for frontier models, and commitments around AI literary and workforce training.

Following an AI researcher’s ominous warning about the technology, lawmakers in Washington scrambled this week to manage the abrupt panic around AI development, floating numerous proposals to prevent its negative potential.

Strategists in the Friday letter argued the technology “poses extreme risks to the public” and “requires clear guardrails to protect Americans and create accountability for tech companies that fail to adhere to basic guardrails.”

Commenting on past proposals, LTF said AI deserves “rigorous debate as Congress works toward durable solutions that protect the public while accelerating American innovation and leadership.”

data.title: Hollywood handouts shouldn't come before environmental cleanup
data.description:
Representatives from both parties are drafting a federal tax incentive for the movie industry — a move likely to give taxpayers a poor return on their money. New evidence highlights the type of spending that benefits communities one can overlook when jetting from Los Angeles to Gotham.

State and local governments have a history of throwing cash at firms to entice them to their jurisdiction. My review of credible studies regarding relocation incentives found that, on average, 93 percent of relocating firms would have come anyway. Incentives for Hollywood fit the pattern. An audit of Georgia’s Film Tax Credit found that for each dollar the state gave, 19 cents came back. Although tax revenue is just one metric, it shows the unfavorable deal taxpayers gave for Hollywood to come down to Georgia.

Governments at all levels should exit the business of ad-hoc corporate tax incentives and focus on what they are uniquely positioned to do: fund broadly enjoyed goods that others won’t. A prime example is funding the cleanup of environmental hazards that plague many communities and the restoration of the amenities they once enjoyed. A corporation can pocket a tax incentive and move on; no one can pocket a river made healthy for fish and people or a site suitable for new homes.

Abandoned mine drainage contaminates as many as 39,000 miles of streams in Appalachia alone. Interviews with residents of mine-affected areas reveal that mine-polluted waterways foster pessimism about the future and neglect in the present, with one type of pollution, mine drainage,  leading to others, trash dumping. People leave such places if they have the chance: from 1990 to 2020, Pennsylvania communities with mine drainage problems and no restoration saw their population decline by 9 percent. That’s almost 1 in 10 people moving elsewhere.

Supported by public funding, grassroots organizations have built and maintained hundreds of wetland systems to treat mine drainage, improving water clarity for miles downstream. Residents near restored waterways report a new sense of pride of place and optimism about the future. As a result, longtime residents stayed and new ones came, especially those with more education. 

The cost? About $240 per resident of a Census tract with restoration. By comparison, the federal Empowerment Zone program, which mainly consisted of business incentives, spent $1,500 per resident and attracted fewer people to select Census tracts.

Treating abandoned mine drainage is one of many possibilities for high-return public investments that cannot be uprooted and offshored. Brownfields are another. Remediating them — assuming no responsible party exists to do it — turns a community hazard into an asset for repurposing. 

An example is Pennsylvania’s Hazardous Sites Cleanup Act program, which helped turn the site of a former steel and coke plant in Pittsburgh into innovation centers and advanced manufacturing facilities. A study of brownfield cleanups showed that by increasing property values they would generate, with reassessments, enough tax revenue in one year to more than cover cleanup costs. Compare that to the Georgia film tax credit that repays 19 cents on the dollar.  

The bipartisan Ohio River Restoration Program Act, sponsored by Sens. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), aims to remediate toxic substances, protect drinking water sources, restore fish and wildlife habitat and create opportunities for public access and recreation. The act won’t produce Hollywood blockbusters, but its proposed funding is $350 million a year. 

Meanwhile, Los Angeles filmmakers flying over the Ohio Valley can tap New York’s film tax credits for up to $700 million a year.

Jeremy G. Weber is professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public and International Affairs and author of “Statistics for Public Policy: A Practical Guide to Being Mostly Right” (or at Least Respectably Wrong), University of Chicago Press.

data.title: Lawmakers salute staffers keeping Capitol Hill afloat: 'Everything is grit and hard work'
data.description:
A bipartisan group of lawmakers highlighted the the integral role of staffers in the daily function of Congress Thursday at The Hill’s annual Notable Staffers event. 

Sens. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) as well as Reps. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Bobby Scott (D-Va.) honored their staffers, all who made this year’s list of the legislative branch’s top aides.

During the panel, moderated by The Hill’s Julia Manchester, the lawmakers said staffers work hard to achieve bipartisan success by reaching consensus between stakeholders and getting bills across the finish line. 

“Everything is grit and hard work and making yourself indispensable and doing things that other people won’t do,” Booker said

Booker added that the ideal character of a staffer isn’t someone with an “entitled” Ivy League degree, but someone who is going to work hard and distinguishes themselves through hard work. 

“When you have a staffer that significant, and who goes home at night and studies to expand the knowledge that he makes available to all of us is truly amazing,” Lummis said of her staffer Chris Land, who she touted as having an integral hand in crafting the bipartisan CLARITY Act regulating the crypto industry. 

Scott, who was there to honor his staffer Carrie Hughs — the health and human services director of the House Education and the Workforce Committee — said passing legislation means speaking to different factions and growing a consensus, which relies on staffers’ good relationships on boths sides of the aisle.

“You have to have people that can get along with people to put together the best coalition you can to get your legislation passed,” Scott said. “Cause ultimately you can have nice legislation but if too many people are opposing it, won’t pass.” 

Raskin — who applauded Nellie Decker, communications director of the House Judiciary Committee Democrats —  said the culture of a good congressional is shaped by staffers. He said members often rely on their staffers to interface with other offices on official business so they can retain their good relationship with other members. 

“The people in the office really come to represent, both literally and metaphorically, the member and they protect us a lot,” Raskin said. 

The New Jersey senator also highlighted that diversity among staff matters can contribute to member’s support for important bills. Booker said Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) once told him that he was signing onto his bill funding Sickle Cell Disease research because the Black members of his staff insisted. Sickle cell disease disproportionately affects Black Americans.

He noted, however, that Congress has to do more to bring in talent from all corners of America. 

“Congress has got to do a lot more to pull the talent from America and present opportunities for America for people who don’t normally serve on the Hill,” Booker said. “That will make this Capitol be far better in doing its job for the American people.

data.title: Senate Republican on campaigning in 'close' red state races: 'These oughta be fat guy layups'
data.description:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said Republicans are facing unexpectedly close Senate races in traditionally red states as the party fights to maintain its majority in November.

Kennedy told reporters Thursday that he plans to travel to Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa this weekend to campaign and raise money for Republican Senate candidates.

“If you told me six months ago I was going to be having to spend my time in those three states, I wouldn’t have believed you,” Kennedy said. “Those oughta be fat guy layups for us.”

“Now we’re gonna win there,” he added. “But the races are close.”

Kennedy said Republicans need to focus their message on inflation and the economy, which have remained top concerns for voters heading into the midterms amid the Iran war.

“We’ve got to talk about the economy. We’ve got to talk about the cost of living,” he said.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, meaning Democrats need to a net gain of four seats for control of the chamber.

The Cook Political Report rates the Senate contests in Kansas and Nebraska as “Likely Republican,” while Iowa is among seven races rated as a “Toss Up.”

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) is seeking a second term against Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, a pastor. Cook moved the race from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican” after Hamilton won the Democratic primary in August. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since the 1930s.

In Nebraska, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) is facing independent Dan Osborn, while Iowa has an open Senate race following Sen. Joni Ernst’s (R-Iowa) decision to retire. Cook moved Iowa into its “Toss Up” category last month.

Kennedy’s comments come as Republicans work to solidify their economic messaging ahead of the midterms. Recent polling shows voters are favoring Democrats over Republicans on their most important issues, including the economy, health care and immigration.

data.title: Second death confirmed in Bronx Legionnaires' disease cluster
data.description:
NEW YORK CITY (WPIX) — A second person has died in connection with the South Bronx Legionnaires’ disease cluster, according to the city’s health commissioner.

“We mourn the loss of each New Yorker, and our hearts are with their loved ones as they navigate this difficult time,” Dr. Alister Martin said on social media.

As of Thursday, 13 people had tested positive for the disease and two were still in the hospital.

Yankee Stadium is among 10 buildings the health department ordered to clean and disinfect their cooling towers.

“We are grateful to our local elected officials who have joined us in outreach efforts as we respond quickly to cut off the exposure and investigate cases. All cooling towers that tested positive through initial screening have been disinfected,” Martin added.

Health officials say it is safe to shower, drink tap water, and use air conditioners in the affected zip codes unless otherwise advised.

This latest cluster comes after 11 people died from an outbreak over the summer on Manhattan’s Upper East Side.

Legionella forms in warm, stagnant water; a cooling tower creates the perfect conditions. Health officials say older adults are at greater risk, but Legionnaires’ disease can also pose a greater threat to people who smoke or vape, those with weakened immune systems, and people with chronic health conditions including heart, lung, kidney or liver disease and diabetes.

data.title: Europe wants Canada in but keeps Turkey out
data.description:
Earlier this week, in her address on the “the State of the Union,” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen announced that the EU would invite Canada to join the organization as an Associate Member. Von der Leyen explained that Europe could “no longer rely on [the rules-based system] as the only way to secure our interests” and that it must therefore “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies.”

She then issued what clearly was intended to be a pointed jab at Washington, and an unambiguous allusion to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call at the World Economic Forum earlier this year that “Middle powers … act together because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.”

Von der Leyen was not as florid, but she made the same point. “We believe,” she said, “that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us … Democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”

For the past eight years Canada and the EU have had a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement that eliminated 99 per cent of tariffs. Von der Leyen said Europe will move from this agreement to “an Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space.” This more comprehensive cooperative arrangement would include intelligent manufacturing; a new “tech alliance;” integrated defense industrial bases; the Arctic as “a flagship joint project” and joint efforts on energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum, cyber and economic security.

“In short,” she summarized, “we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.” To that end she invited Canada to become the “first associate member of the EU.”

Except that it is not the first. Turkey has been an associate member for over six decades.

The 1963 Ankara Agreement that Turkey and the European Economic Community (the EU’s predecessor) signed in 1963 provided for Turkey’s associate membership. It envisaged a not only the creation of a customs union between them, but the country’s eventual membership in the organization. Seven years later, both sides signed an additional protocol that outlined a long-term schedule for the full implementation of the Customs Union but did not address membership.

The Customs Union finally came into force in 1995. Turkey had applied for membership in 1987, but the European Commission rejected the application two years later. Only in 1999 did the European Union finally agree to give Turkey candidate status. In other words, it accepted the principle that Turkey would someday become an EU member. That day has yet to arrive.

There are numerous reasons the EU has dragged its feet on Turkish membership, starting with concerns about Turkey’s human rights record. For years, Greece also opposed Turkish entry, but it dropped its opposition in 1999.

There continues to be friction over Cyprus, an EU member. Turkey alone recognizes the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which the United Nations considers a breakaway entity from the Republic of Cyprus. For their part, Turks assert that, in the words of a leading Turkish expert, “the EU created the Greek State of Cyprus.”

There is also popular European opposition to Turkish entry. Turkey’s population of over 85 million swamps that of many EU states — it is equal in size to ten smaller EU members combined.

There is no indication that Turkey will join the EU any time soon. All of the factors that have generated European governments’ and public opposition remain in place. Indeed, the rise of anti-immigration and especially anti-Muslim feeling in much of Europe has only hardened opposition to Turkish entry into the EU.

In contrast, whereas the Canadian government has not yet expressed interest in joining the EU, once it becomes an Associate Member, the door to entry theoretically opens.

As a former British colony and dominion, an independent member of the British Commonwealth, and a founding member of NATO, Canada has always reached out across the Atlantic. Canada’s new arrangement with the EU simply marks another milestone in that long standing relationship. Yet association with the EU is a direct outcome of Canadian friction with the U.S. and Ottawa’s determination both to diversify its international economic relationships and to loosen its ties to what it perceives to be a menacing southern neighbor.

The EU has extended a warm hand to Canada’s recent outreach. Meanwhile, it keeps the door closed to Turkey, despite its longstanding desire for membership, and despite its NATO membership. Sadly, this reflects Europe’s deep-seated fear of forging closer economic and social ties with a powerful and populous Muslim state that is no longer the “sick man of Europe” it once was.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987.

data.title: Former Institute of Peace board members ask court to stop addition of Trump name to headquarters
data.description:
Ousted former board members for the U.S. Institute of Peace asked a federal court on Thursday to block the Trump administration from etching President Trump’s name into the facade at the building’s headquarters in Washington, D.C.

In an emergency petition filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, lawyers for the former institute leadership alleged the administration “now intends to carve” Trump’s name into the building. 

“The threatened carving would impose serious irreparable harm,” the attorneys wrote in their filing. “It is a discrete act that can and should be forestalled through a limited, status-quo-preserving modification of the stay pending appeal.” 

The president’s name was already added to the building’s exterior in removable silver lettering in December. The institute’s name is carved into the facade. 

The Hill has reached out to the White House about whether there are plans to engrave the president’s name. 

The institute was one of the many organizations targeted for cuts by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency — an effort that sparked an ongoing legal battle. 

Congress created the institute in 1984 and allocates federal funding for its programs. The institute’s headquarters building was built using a mix of private donations and federal money. 

“The building — which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation — is a work of expressive architecture designed to be ‘symbolic of USIP’s’ independent ‘mission,’” the attorneys wrote in their filing. 

The president has sought to affix his name to several other historic buildings and monuments around the nation’s capital. 

Trump’s efforts to take over the Kennedy Center have been subjected to ongoing litigation after he fired half of the performing arts center’s board, named himself as its new chair and pushed to add his name to the side of the iconic building. 

After a federal judge blocked this renaming effort on Tuesday, the president announced that the Kennedy Center would be closing “so that it can begin the process of Reconstruction.”

data.title: Judge strikes down anti-DEI grant policy at Education Department
data.description:
A federal judge ruled Thursday the Education Department cannot cut money to teacher training programs the Trump administration argues are focused on “divisive ideologies.” 

In February 2025, the department moved to slash around $600 million to grants it didn’t like under the Teacher Quality Partnership and Supporting Effective Educator Development grant programs. 

District Judge Angel Kelley said the directive was “arbitrary and capricious” due to its failure to explain the switch in grants that previously encouraged “DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion] programs.” 

“Rather than confining the Directive to actions that are traditionally understood to constitute discrimination, the record instead reflects that Defendants terminated grants with topics such as ‘acknowledging . . . racism’ and ‘anti-racism’—activities expressly undertaken to oppose discrimination,” Kelley wrote. 

She also objected to the directive due to the impact it would have on teacher preparation. 

The Hill has reached out to the Education Department for comment.  

The challenge to the move came from Democratic states, which previously had the directive halted by a federal judge, but the Supreme Court in April 2025 said the department could continue the cuts while the case proceeded in court. 

In 2025, the Education Department said the slash in funds was directed towards programs focused on critical race theory, DEI, social justice, anti-racism, white privilege and white supremacy.   

Examples of grant applications the department objected to included one with a description that required “practitioners to take personal and institutional responsibility for systemic inequities (e.g., racism) and critically reassess their own practices.”

data.title: White House set to tout Medicaid most favored nation drug pricing deals
data.description:
President Trump on Friday is set to announce that all 50 states will see most favored nation (MFN) pricing for some drugs in Medicaid, according to an administration official.

Trump will be joined by “several governors” in the Oval Office to make the announcement, the official said. 

With affordability a top concern among voters, Republicans hope to use drug pricing as a winning message in a November’s midterm elections. 

“Today’s announcement confirms that every state Medicaid program will save billions on prescription drug costs thanks to President Trump,” the White House official said. 

The administration’s GENEROUS model allows participating states to purchase drugs at a price aligned with those paid in other countries. The theory, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, is that it will allow state Medicaid programs to benefit from fairer, more competitive pricing.

The administration has suggested state Medicaid programs could save more than $64 billion, but it’s not clear how they arrived at that figure. 

Medicaid drugs are already subject to steep discounts, so the impact of MFN agreements on drug costs and accessibility isn’t clear.

data.title: The Fed is fighting the wrong war on inflation
data.description:
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates this week, pushing the federal funds rate to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent. That decision will not produce more oil, reopen disrupted shipping lanes or remove tariffs that are raising production costs. It can, however, weaken investment, hiring and wage growth.

Before imposing those costs, policymakers should ask whether they are fighting the inflation we actually have. The crucial question is not simply whether inflation is too high, but why prices are rising and whether higher interest rates can address the source of the problem.

Much of the recent increase reflects supply pressures. Conflicts disrupting global energy flows have pushed up oil and gasoline prices, raising costs throughout the economy. In August, gasoline prices rose 3.9 percent and accounted for more than one-third of the increase in the Consumer Price Index.

Those increases do not just remain at the pump, either. Energy is an input into nearly everything we produce and consume, so higher fuel costs eventually appear even in core inflation measures that do not include energy directly.

A price-level increase caused by a supply shock is not the same as a continuing inflationary process. If oil rises from $70 to $100 a barrel and then remains there, gasoline, production and transportation costs rise while the economy adjusts. Once that adjustment is complete, the oil increase alone does not keep generating inflation. Oil would have to continue rising, or the initial shock would have to set off repeated increases in wages and other prices.  

The Fed is right to worry that an initial shock could spread. In the 1970s, oil shocks became embedded as wages and prices reinforced one another. But that history does not justify treating every oil shock as the beginning of another wage-price spiral. It raises a harder question: How much economic activity should the Fed deliberately sacrifice to prevent a supply shock from spreading, and what evidence shows that this tradeoff is already necessary?

Higher rates can restrain demand, but only indirectly. Higher borrowing costs discourage consumption and investment, slow construction and business expansion, and reduce pressure in the labor market. Softer demand then gives firms less room to pass higher costs on to consumers. That is how monetary policy can keep a supply shock from broadening. It works by suppressing spending, investment, hiring and wage growth elsewhere in the economy.  

That mechanism matters, because the Fed has another mandate: maximum employment. The labor market remains healthy, but it is hardly so overheated that it requires deliberate cooling. Unemployment was 4.1 percent in August, but employment growth has slowed considerably from earlier in the recovery. If higher rates reduce inflation driven largely by energy and tariffs, they will do so by restraining the broader economy and putting jobs at risk.

If excessive demand were driving an accelerating inflationary process, tighter policy would be appropriate. But when energy disruptions and tariffs are raising costs, the Fed risks attacking the wrong problem. It cannot lower the price of oil, but it can make businesses less willing to invest, employers less willing to hire and households less willing to finance major purchases such as homes, vehicles and durable goods. 

That does not mean the Fed should ignore inflation. Policymakers should act if the shock begins feeding into accelerating wages, rising long-run inflation expectations and broad price increases across sectors that are not directly exposed to higher energy or tariff costs. Those are the signs that a temporary price shock is becoming a self-reinforcing inflationary process.  

Right now, the data do not show that pattern. Wage growth has slowed substantially from its pandemic peak, while unit labor costs, which measure labor compensation relative to productivity, rose just 1.2 percent in the second quarter of 2026. Meanwhile, long-run inflation expectations do not indicate that households expect today’s inflation to persist indefinitely. Taken together, these indicators do not suggest that wages, labor costs and expectations are beginning to reinforce one another in a self-sustaining inflationary cycle.  

Without clearer evidence that wage and price pressures are broadening or that inflation expectations are becoming unanchored, the Fed should hold — even if markets have come to expect further tightening. 

The Fed should not tighten against the possibility that inflation will spread without evidence that it is actually spreading. Uncomfortable inflation numbers are not enough. Higher interest rates cannot reverse an external supply shock. They can only restrain the rest of the economy in an effort to contain it. Whether that tradeoff is justified depends on the data, not market expectations.

B. Oak McCoy is assistant professor of economics at the University of New England.
